messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol had been 27 when she first came to treatment, a single HVAC technician in a city where she spent most days crawling through attics, basements, and apartment closets, places that left her alone with customers longer than she liked. The event she kept returning to had happened during a short period of detention years earlier, when she was held in a windowless room and made to feel that there were no options, no one coming, and no way to control what happened next. What stayed with her was not only the pain but the humiliation of being watched while injured, and the way the fear sharpened whenever a woman entered the room or stood too close while she was vulnerable. In the present, even a routine service call could put her on edge if she found herself alone with a female client in a confined laundry room or hallway, because those moments carried the same trapped feeling; visible injuries on other people, especially cuts or bruises, could also stop her cold, as if she were back in that room again, staring at someone hurt and unable to do anything.

Afterward, Marisol became convinced that danger could come from anywhere, from anyone. She said she had come to believe that you could never know who would harm you, and that this had changed her for good. She also doubted her own judgment, worrying that she could not trust herself to do the right thing if something went wrong, and that she had permanently changed for the worse. Those beliefs fed directly into the way she lived: when she arrived home from work she checked the doors and windows again and again, not because she expected a break-in every night but because she no longer trusted her own sense that a place was secure. At bedtime she would wake in the dark and listen, then move through the apartment to check the locks before she could settle again. She described herself as jumpy on the job too, flinching when a compressor kicked on or a customer came up behind her, her body seeming to react before she had time to think.

The memory itself was another force in the same pattern. When it came back, Marisol said it felt alien, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her, and the shame that came with recalling it was intense enough that she would cut herself off mid-thought. At times the emotion rose so fast that she had to stop talking altogether, look away, and take a breath before she could continue. Those moments made her even more certain that something was wrong with her, and the sense of being permanently altered only deepened her fear that she could not depend on her own decisions or keep herself safe. When the memory surged, the room, her body, and the old helplessness all blurred together, and the immediate effect was to make her scan for exits, check a latch, or back away from whatever had set it off.

The more she monitored for danger, the more tightly the world narrowed around those same cues. Being alone with women became harder to tolerate because it brought back the old sense of being confined and exposed, and she would find excuses to step outside, send a text, or wait until another coworker arrived. Seeing injuries on others carried the same punch, and she began to avoid situations where she might have to stand close to someone hurt or bleeding. Over time, that caution started to shape her workday; she took longer routes through buildings, avoided certain call orders, and felt increasingly unsettled in customer homes where a closed door or narrow hallway made escape feel uncertain. Each time she noticed her heart racing or her attention locking onto a door, it seemed to confirm that her fear was justified, which in turn made her watch for the very things that scared her. By the time she sought help, Marisol was exhausted by the repeated checking, the broken sleep, and the shrinking circle of places she felt able to enter, and what frightened her most was that her own mind seemed to keep proving her right. At the same time, she hoped therapy might help her understand why the memory still felt so foreign and shameful, and whether she could learn to trust herself again without feeling as though she were always one step away from danger.
